name: failure
description: Dismay caused by a sense that you were not able to achieve a desired outcome after making a mistake of action or inaction.
perceptions: An outcome I had desired did not happen.
It's my fault that it didn't happen.

guidance.description: Whether you were denied a promotion at the office or you didn't qualify for a marathon, failing feels bad. Many people will go to great lengths to avoid failing so they don’t have to feel painful emotions.

variations.name: garden variety failure
variations.description: A perception that it's your fault a desired outcome did not happen, along with a perception that you can learn from the event.
perceptions: Something I had valued is gone or not available.
It's my fault that it's gone.
results: considering ways to do better next time
examples: not scoring well on the homework assignment
breaking a favorite cup while washing it

variations.name: repeated failure
variations.description: A perception that it's your fault an outcome did not happen, along with a perception that you have had this failure before.
perceptions: Something I had valued is gone or not available.
It's my fault that it's gone.
I've done this more than once and have not yet learned.
examples: not scoring well on multiple homework assignments
repeatedly breaking dishes while washing them

guidance.description: there are so many skills in life that you can only become an expert and some skills you can’t even do until you’ve failed. Repeatedly. Over and over.

variations.name: failure sickness
variations.description: A perception that it's your fault a desired outcome did not happen, and that this loss brings shame to a social identity.
perceptions: Something I had valued is gone or not available.
It's my fault that it's gone.

guidance.description: See the guidance entry for shame.

variations.name: failure in others
variations.description: Disappointment in the actions of others whom you had hoped would not lose.
perceptions: Something I had valued is gone or not available.
The person who's responsible for the loss was someone I had hoped would not lose.
results: consider how to respond to the failure

guidance.description: Sometimes, it may be good to let people fail

examples: kid struck out to lose a close game

variations.name: burnout
variations.description: A state of anxiety and failure after exhausting yourself on a large project without finishing it.
perceptions: I've been working on this big project for a long time.
I'm anxious and don't think I can complete it.

guidance.description: Too much change, too many demands, and eventually the human mind and body will cave in under all the pressure. Here are some tips to get yourself and your life back, ASAP.

examples: Deadline for the big project approaching and too much to do.

comparisons.description: Failure is a loss where you blame yourself.
Regret is when you're disappointed in the outcome of a perceived failure and not so focused on your actions that may have led to the failure.
Guilt is when you're hard on yourself for a perceived failure in something socially or morally important, probably in an effort to avoid repeating it.

Shame is the social sense that something is deeply, almost morally, wrong with yourself. Failure is an instance of something that didn't go as well as it could have. It may well be that a failure should cause shame. Or it may be that your shame circuits are too sensitive.

commentaries.quote: Some of us are all too ready to blame ourselves for small things. Others are unwilling to recognize even big mistakes.
Fear of failure can keep us from trying anything.

Failure is often framed as a great teacher—the successful sometimes crow about the number of times they failed before hitting it big. But failure may not always teach us as much as it could, often because ego gets in the way.
commentaries.attribution: Alice G. Walton in 'Learn by Failing? Not So Easy'

commentaries.quote: Brain patterns cannot get better without the recalibration that comes from both success and failure. But likewise, the patterns won't get better if we're not honest with ourselves.

There's a well known mantra that successful companies “fail fast and often.” This glib saying masks a few sobering realities. First, failure triggers our fight or flight response, so we are hardwired to avoid it. Even young children are quick to avoid blame in the face of a mishap. Second, learning from it contradicts human nature: extensive research shows that we learn from other people's failures, but when it comes to ourselves, we glean insights only from our successes.
